questions.stem: The most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere (by volume) is:
questions.explanation: Dry air by volume — Nitrogen 78.09 %, Oxygen 20.95 %, Argon 0.93 %, CO₂ ~0.04 %. Trace gases — Ne, He, Kr, Xe. Water vapour varies from near zero to ~4 %. Plants get nitrogen from the soil (fixed by rhizobium bacteria in legumes, lightning, industrial Haber process), not directly from the air.

questions.stem: The lightest gas, used in weather balloons because it is not flammable (unlike the next-lightest), is:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is the lightest element but flammable — the Hindenburg disaster (1937). Helium (second-lightest, inert and non-flammable) is therefore preferred for weather balloons, airships and children's party balloons. Produced on Earth from natural-gas wells rich in radioactive decay helium. Neon is used in signs (red-orange glow); methane (CH₄) is the main component of natural gas and is highly flammable.

questions.stem: The gas produced as a by-product of photosynthesis in plants is:
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + sunlight → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6 O₂. Plants take CO₂ in and give O₂ out during the day. At night they also respire, which consumes O₂ and releases CO₂ — but the daytime oxygen output is larger. Cellular respiration (in all aerobic organisms, including plants) is the reverse reaction.

questions.stem: 'Laughing gas' — an anaesthetic used in dentistry — is chemically:
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide (N₂O) — 'laughing gas' — used as a mild anaesthetic and sedative, especially in dentistry, since the 19th century. It produces euphoria (hence the name) followed by analgesia. A potent greenhouse gas (~300 times stronger than CO₂ per kg). NO and NO₂ are 'NOₓ' — pollutants from vehicles; NH₃ is ammonia.

questions.stem: The gas that gives a rotten-egg smell is:
questions.explanation: H₂S has the characteristic rotten-egg smell; toxic at even small concentrations, potentially fatal at higher ones; detectable by the human nose at just 0.0005 ppm. Found around decaying organic matter, volcanoes, hot springs, rotten eggs. SO₂ has a sharp, acrid smell (burning matches). Chlorine has a pungent, bleach-like smell. Methane is odourless — LPG suppliers add ethyl mercaptan (ethanethiol) to give it a warning smell.

questions.stem: At standard temperature and pressure (STP: 0 °C and 1 atm), one mole of any gas occupies approximately:
questions.explanation: Avogadro's law + ideal gas law — at STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole (6.022 × 10²³ molecules) of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L. At 25 °C and 1 atm ('NTP' / 'ambient conditions' in the newer IUPAC definition of STP at 100 kPa) the molar volume is slightly different (~24.5 L). 11.2 L is half a mole at STP; 44.8 L is 2 moles.

questions.stem: Which of the following gases is a major contributor to acid rain?
questions.explanation: SO₂ (from burning sulphur-rich coal and oil, from smelters) combines with water and oxygen in the atmosphere to form sulphuric acid — the dominant component of acid rain. NOₓ from vehicle exhaust also forms nitric acid and adds to acid rain. Acid rain damages forests, fish populations and historical stonework (the Taj Mahal being a famous victim). Methane is a greenhouse gas; noble gases are essentially inert.
